risk_of_bias.note: Measurement (card sc_davis_2020b, JBI prevalence checklist, high): a study-specific questionnaire without validation; one report of the single most memorable encounter, on average about 4.6 years earlier (editors' calculation); 'before' religious identification recalled in the same sitting as 'after'; lasting changes are respondents' attributions, not measured change; half of the eligible people who consented did not complete (4,610 of 9,179 did), and those who did not are not described; item non-response is not reported; open-ended answers were coded by the authors (94% to 95% agreement on a 20% subsample). The God-encounter survey (card sc_griffiths_2019, JBI prevalence checklist, high) has the same kinds of problems: study-made items without reported validation; the single most memorable encounter recalled on average 11.0 years later (20.5 years in the no-drug group); religion 'before' rated at the survey; attributed rather than measured change; and 5,165 of the 11,023 who met its criteria did not finish (47%, editors' calculation) and are not described.

inconsistency.note: Not rated down. Where the two surveys asked the same questions about DMT experiences, the answers point the same way (communication 84% and 80%; a message 69% and 74%; predictions 19% and 21%; atheist identification falling from 28% to 10% and from 25% to 7%), while some shares differ (two-way communication 40% and 28%; continued to exist 72% and 53%; among the five most personally meaningful experiences 55% and 81%), plausibly because one survey sampled entity encounters and the other encounters taken to be God or Ultimate Reality; each sample is described separately and nothing is pooled.

indirectness.note: Coverage: only people who reported an encounter could take part, recruited mainly through DMT and drug websites, in English; 2,049 completers were excluded (psychotic disorder, other substances, other routes, changa, data quality), and each described only the most memorable encounter. The shares describe this filtered group, not people who use DMT, not all encounters, and not experiences with ayahuasca or DMT taken another way. The God-encounter survey required an encounter that people took to be God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God, named in the purpose given to everyone; it does not name its recruitment sources, and its no-drug and psychedelic groups were recruited into separate versions of the questionnaire and differ in age, sex and recalled religion. Its shares describe those groups, and its DMT group's encounters were selected as God encounters, not entity encounters as such.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: 2,561 respondents give shares precise to about plus or minus 2 percentage points, and the God-encounter survey's groups of 809 and 606 to about 3 to 4 points (editors' calculations); its no-drug share of former atheists who no longer identified as atheist rests on about 24 people (editors' arithmetic) and is imprecise, but nothing here rests on that share alone.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for two surveys from one group.

rate.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports what respondents said they experienced and believed; it makes no claim that the beings exist, that the messages or predictions are true, or that the experience caused the changes in belief or well-being that respondents attributed to it, which a single cross-sectional report cannot show, as its authors state. The abstract's conclusion that aspects of the experience produced profound and enduring changes in worldview is not adopted as a causal finding, and the suggestion that DMT could help in therapy was not tested. Companion papers of 12 November: the authors' earlier God-encounter survey (Griffiths et al., 2019; card sc_griffiths_2019, JBI prevalence checklist, high), read in full, supplies the comparison that the entity survey reported only as t-tests (p < 0.001), with each group's numbers and denominators, and a group whose encounters happened without any drug: a communicating, intelligent, mostly benevolent presence, messages and a fall in recalled atheist identification are reported without drugs too, so these kinds of report are not specific to DMT. Its recruitment cannot represent how often such encounters happen, people who would not answer a long English online survey whose stated purpose named God, or typical rather than most memorable experiences; its group differences are descriptive, because the groups were recruited into separate versions and differ in age, sex and recalled religion before the experience (not adjusted), and its authors say it cannot separate DMT's pharmacology from expectation and context. It shares the entity survey's limits, so the rating stays very low. Status replicated by the same team: where the two surveys asked the same questions about DMT experiences the answers point the same way, but the surveys share investigators, a questionnaire and online recruitment, so they are not independent replication (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence); the labels (being, guide, spirit, alien, elf) rest on the entity survey alone. Published descriptions of experiences without drugs, which the entity survey cites, are still not used. The breakthrough criterion and the route are reported as study conditions only.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns (card sc_studerus_2021): each predictor adjusted only for dose per kilogram, correlated predictors not adjusted for one another, blinding probably did not hold at 125 mg, the text does not say whether ratings were placebo-corrected, so rating style could add to trait-rating associations, and the 5D-ASC ratings were made at the end of the session, looking back.

inconsistency.note: One pooled analysis. On sex, the authors cite an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017) among studies suggesting women may be more prone to unpleasant effects; the two analyses share most of their data and are not independent, so this is stated in the claim rather than rated as inconsistency.

indirectness.note: Worded for healthy laboratory volunteers taking one known dose; real-life use is named as different in the statement.

imprecision.note: 194 people; corrected significance throughout; modest variance shares stated.

publication_bias.note: All 500 adjusted tests are said to be displayed and corrected.

rate.reasoning: The MDMA-placebo contrast was randomized in each source study, but which person's characteristics predict the response is a between-person, observational question, so it starts low; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: one pooled analysis from one laboratory; other Basel pooled analyses share these source studies and its LSD counterpart shares one study and several authors, so they are not independent confirmation. On sex, the answer on what MDMA feels like reports the earlier analysis (higher bad-effect ratings in women after allowing for dose per kilogram); in the editors' reading the difference may come from the outcome measure (area under the effect curve here, peak ratings there) and from the correction for multiple testing applied here, and it is listed for the senior author.

rate.comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at the same dose per kilogram (placebo sessions in the same people)
rate.outcome: Self-rated and physical effects of MDMA (visual analogue scales over the session; 5D-ASC rated at the end of the session, looking back; Adjective Mood Rating Scale; blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, blood level)

rate.short: Yes. The biggest link was the amount per kilo of body weight. Given the same amount, lighter people got more per kilo, which went with stronger effects.
rate.rate: Ten pooled studies from one lab, with 194 healthy volunteers. It compares people who differ in many ways, so it shows links, not causes, and each link was modest.

inconsistency.note: Both versions of the strip detected xylazine near 1 to 2.5 µg/mL; they differ on lidocaine, which the change of antibody explains.

indirectness.note: Residues swabbed from used equipment, one production lot, laboratory readers; the claim is about xylazine strips as people use them on powders or pills.

imprecision.note: 38 and 34 classified samples (intervals 86.5–99.5% and 89.8–100%); 15 strips per concentration for the limit; cross-reactivity rests on two strips per compound at one concentration, which is stated in the claim.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

rate.exposure: One production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips, two strips per sample, read in a laboratory; a later version with a different antibody in a second study
rate.comparator: GC-MS/MS quantitation of xylazine in each residue sample; known content of prepared solutions
rate.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity on residue samples, the lowest concentration giving consistent positives, and reactions to other compounds
rate.magnitude: Sisco, Nestadt, et al. (2024), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%; the one miss at 2 µg/mL); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). (2024), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.
rate.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
rate.rate: Two lab studies by one team. The 97-in-100 figure leaves out samples with only a little xylazine, and no one tried the strips on street powders or pills, or outside a lab.

lines.statement: In 2,561 adults who answered an anonymous online survey in 2018 after recruitment through websites and forums (for example reddit, dmt-nexus, bluelight and drugs-forum) and by email (mean age 31.9; 77% men; 85% White; 64% living in the USA; a median of 6 lifetime DMT uses), all of whom reported at least one encounter with a seemingly autonomous being or entity (the study's term) after a 'breakthrough' dose of DMT (defined as one with very strong effects), smoked or vaporized without other substances, and each describing their single most memorable encounter, on average about 4.6 years earlier (editors' calculation from the mean ages now and at the experience), the respondents reported the following (Davis et al., 2020). Only people who reported an encounter could take part, so the survey cannot show how often encounters happen; of the 9,179 eligible people who consented, 4,610 completed the survey and affirmed their answers, and 2,049 of these (editors' sum) were then excluded, by design (103 with a psychotic disorder diagnosis, 1,279 who had taken other substances that may have affected the experience, 457 who took DMT another way) or for duplicate addresses, undisclosed substance use, use of changa or inattentive answers (34 and 176). For 67% the encounter described was their first. They reported mainly seeing (92%) and extrasensory, for example telepathic, contact (85%); 84% reported communication with the entity, 40% two-way and 49% one-way from the entity, most often by telepathy (74%). From a list (all that apply), they called it a being (60%), guide (43%), spirit (39%), alien (39%), helper (34%), angel (16%), elf (14%), religious personage (11%), plant spirit (10%), fairy (8%), clown (6%), demon (6%) or deceased family member (2%), among other labels. During the encounter they felt joy (65%), trust (63%), surprise (61%), love (59%), kindness (56%), friendship (48%) and fear (41%); love was most often the single most prominent emotion (21%), fear for 7%, and 32% rated it, psychologically, among the five most challenging experiences of their lives. Rated moderately or more, the entity seemed conscious (96%), intelligent (96%), benevolent (78%) and sacred (70%), and malicious to 11%. Looking back from now, 65% judged the experience more real than everyday waking consciousness (81% as it felt at the time); 49% placed the entity in some real but different dimension or reality, 26% there and in everyday physical reality, 9% completely within themselves and 1% only in everyday reality; 72% believed it continued to exist after the encounter; and 80% said the experience altered their fundamental conception of reality (60% of all respondents called the change desirable, 1% undesirable). 69% (1,773) said they received a message, task, mission, purpose or insight, which the authors coded into themes, most often idiosyncratic information (703), personal insight (571) and love (409); 19% (484) said they received a prediction about the future, most often about a personal life event (156), which the authors call unverifiable with their method. Asked in the same sitting about their religious identification before the encounter and now, 28% recalled being atheist before and 10% said they were atheist now; agnostic 27% and 16%; a belief in ultimate reality, a higher power, God or universal divinity 36% and 58% (each change p < 0.001 by z-tests for paired proportions with Bonferroni correction; no cross-tabulation printed), so at least 64% of those who recalled being atheist no longer identified as atheist (editors' arithmetic; the abstract says more than half). Most attributed lasting positive changes to the experience, for example in well-being or life satisfaction (89%) and life's purpose (82%), and 1% to 5% negative changes, with nothing measured before the experience and no comparison group. The abstract concludes that the experience and how people interpreted it brought deep and lasting changes in their worldview, and the Discussion presents the survey as strong evidence of such changes, while the limitations say that the cross-sectional design 'makes causal interpretations impossible' and cannot show whether the sample represents people who use DMT; the authors add that harms may be underestimated, because people whose lives had been seriously disrupted by such an experience may have been less inclined to take part, and each person described only their most memorable experience. All of these are the respondents' reports and beliefs, not findings about whether such beings exist. The study was funded by a US National Institute on Drug Abuse training grant, the Heffter Research Institute and the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research (itself funded by a private foundation and individual donors); the authors declared no conflicts of interest. A separate, earlier online survey by the same Johns Hopkins group (Griffiths et al., 2019), whose questionnaire the entity survey adapted, sets such reports beside experiences without drugs. Anonymous and unpaid, it recruited through internet advertisements, email invitations and online social networks that it does not name (2014 to 2016; dates printed as 12/03/2014–08/01/2016) adults who reported an encounter with what they took to be God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God (the purpose stated to everyone named these); each described their single most memorable encounter in one of two versions of the questionnaire, one for an encounter without any drug, by people who had never had one after a drug, and one for an encounter after a psychedelic. Of 12,725 who began, 1,702 did not meet the criteria, 5,165 did not finish (47% of the 11,023 who met them; editors' calculation) and 1,573 were excluded for other reasons (editors' sum), leaving 4,285: 809 without drugs and 3,476 after a psychedelic, of whom 606 after DMT other than ayahuasca (mostly smoked), 435 after ayahuasca, 1,184 after psilocybin and 1,251 after LSD. The no-drug group averaged 56.2 years of age and was 27% men, its experiences on average 20.5 years before the survey; the DMT group averaged 30.0 years and was 82% men, 4.7 years (the entity survey: 31.9 years, 77% men, about 4.6 years). Comparisons were adjusted for eight demographic factors but not for religion before the experience, which, as recalled, was Christian, Jewish or Islamic for 47% of the no-drug group and 7% of the DMT group. Shares of the no-drug group (809) and the DMT group (606), with the differences the authors call significant (p ≤ 0.001) marked: communication with what was encountered 63% and 80% (significant), two-way 22% and 28%; a message, task, mission or insight 78% and 74%; predictions about the future 21% and 21%; visual 48% and 83% (significant); best descriptor God 41% and 16% and Ultimate Reality 26% and 48% (both significant), Higher Power 15% and 25%; benevolent (kind, compassionate, altruistic) 86% and 75%; intelligent 80% and 87% (significant); malicious 1% and 8% (significant); existing at least partly in some other dimension or reality 68% and 76% (significant); continuing to exist after the encounter 74% and 53% (significant); among their five most personally meaningful experiences 74% and 81%, and among the five most psychologically challenging 32% and 47%; attributed change in well-being or life satisfaction, mean 2.38 and 2.26 (−3 to +3). Atheist identification, rated at the survey for before and after the encounter, fell from 3% to 1% in the no-drug group and from 25% to 7% in the DMT group; of those who recalled being atheist, 74% in the no-drug group and 67% across all psychedelic groups (about 24 and about 730 people; editors' arithmetic) no longer identified as atheist, a difference the authors found not significant. The entity survey reported its comparison with this DMT group only as significantly lower ratings of meaning, spiritual significance and lasting positive effects (t-tests, p < 0.001); the God-encounter DMT group's numbers against the entity survey's are personal meaning 6.97 against 6.3 and spiritual significance 7.14 against 6.5 (1 to 8), attributed well-being 2.26 against 2.0, and among the five most personally meaningful experiences 81% against 55%, spiritually significant 85% against 65% and psychologically challenging 47% against 32%; two-way communication was 28% against 40% (the entity survey's Discussion describes about 80% in both surveys as two-way communication, a figure that matches any communication, 80% and 84%), and the entity survey did not offer God, ultimate reality or higher power as labels, so the labels cannot be compared. The God-encounter authors say that the survey cannot tell whether the DMT group's differences from the psilocybin and LSD groups reflect the drug or expectation and context, and that popular beliefs about DMT entity encounters may have biased people who use DMT toward having them; their stated limitations are self-reports collected on average more than a decade later, possible social desirability, a long, unpaid, anonymous survey that could have selected the sample, unknown representativeness and 1% Black respondents, and they state that descriptive studies cannot settle whether God exists. The research was funded mainly by the Council on Spiritual Practices, whose convener was a co-author, and the Heffter Research Institute, on whose board the first author served, as the paper declares. As in the entity survey, these are reports and beliefs of people recruited because they had such an encounter: the survey cannot show how often such encounters happen, with or without drugs, or that a drug caused any feature or change. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (two surveys from one group, sharing a questionnaire, so not independent).

Published descriptions of experiences without drugs, which the entity survey cites, are still not used. The breakthrough criterion and the route are reported as study conditions only.

lines.q: What do people say they meet on DMT?
lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part. So we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before DMT, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.
lines.q_on_site_now: What do people say they meet on DMT?

lines.statement: In 194 healthy, screened volunteers aged 18 to 45, four in five new to MDMA, who took MDMA by mouth lying in a quiet hospital ward in Basel, with a placebo on another day (10 double-blind crossover studies pooled by the laboratory that ran them; a single dose in each analysed session, 125 mg for 164 people and 75 mg for 30, the same for women and men, as study conditions; 112 of them also took MDMA in another session after a medicine given first, which was not analysed; Studerus et al., 2021), the amount taken per kilogram of body weight and the blood level went most with how strongly the effects were felt, as the volunteers rated them. Without adjustment, the blood level was associated with the rating of any drug effect (standardized beta 0.48), and in penalized models dose per kilogram was selected for 21 of 25 effects and ranked first for 12, among them any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, feeling stimulated and liking, but mattered less for unpleasant or anxious reactions. At the same dose per kilogram, genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 went with a higher blood level (beta −0.19), older age with a smaller rise in heart rate (−0.27), higher openness with more closeness to others (0.28) and oceanic boundlessness (0.22), higher neuroticism (rated at screening) and trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution (0.32 each) and impaired control (0.26 each), and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before the dose with more anxiety (0.25 and 0.23); oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, impaired control and anxiety were rated on a questionnaire at the end of the session, looking back over it. Each of these associations survived correction for multiple testing and was modest, explaining 5 to 12% of the variation (semi-partial R2). For a rating of a bad drug effect, older age, trait anxiety and anxious-depressed mood before the dose ranked highest in the penalized models, but the association with age did not survive correction for multiple testing in the main models. Women and men did not differ significantly once dose per kilogram was allowed for; because everyone took a fixed amount and women weighed less, women received more per kilogram, so sex and dose per kilogram went together and cannot be cleanly separated in these data (dose per kilogram varied from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg across the volunteers). The authors note that this does not confirm earlier studies that found differences between women and men even after adjusting for body weight, and they cite others, among them an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), suggesting that women may be more prone to unpleasant effects, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people detected no differences between women and men. Previous MDMA use showed no association, but no one had used it more than five times before the study. Expectations were not among the measures, and the setting, highly standardized, could not be studied. So differences between bodies went with feeling more or less from the same amount: at a fixed amount a lighter body meant more per kilogram, which went with stronger effects, and genetically lower enzyme activity went with a higher blood level; each analysed session had one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in a separate answer). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Healthy, screened adults aged 18 to 45, mostly new to MDMA, given MDMA in a hospital ward in 10 pooled laboratory studies (194 people)
lines.exposure: Dose per kilogram and, without adjustment, blood level; characteristics measured before dosing: sex, age, CYP2D6 genetic activity score, previous MDMA use, personality at screening, trait anxiety (timing not stated) and mood just before the dose
lines.comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at the same dose per kilogram (placebo sessions in the same people)
lines.outcome: Self-rated and physical effects of MDMA (visual analogue scales over the session; 5D-ASC rated at the end of the session, looking back; Adjective Mood Rating Scale; blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, blood level)
lines.magnitude: Unadjusted: blood level and any drug effect beta 0.48. Penalized models: dose per kilogram selected for 21 of 25 responses, first for 12. Adjusted for dose per kilogram and corrected for multiple testing: CYP2D6 genetic activity score and blood level −0.19 (R2 0.10); age and heart-rate rise −0.27 (R2 0.07); openness and closeness 0.28 (R2 0.08), oceanic boundlessness 0.22 (R2 0.06); neuroticism and trait anxiety and dread of ego dissolution 0.32 each (R2 0.12 and 0.11), impaired control 0.26 each; anxious-depressed and introverted mood before the dose and 5D-ASC anxiety 0.25 and 0.23 (R2 0.06 and 0.05). Age and bad drug effect: first in the penalized model, not significant after correction. Sex and previous MDMA use (at most five times): no significant association after adjustment.
lines.reasoning: The MDMA-placebo contrast was randomized in each source study, but which person's characteristics predict the response is a between-person, observational question, so it starts low; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: one pooled analysis from one laboratory; other Basel pooled analyses share these source studies and its LSD counterpart shares one study and several authors, so they are not independent confirmation. On sex, the answer on what MDMA feels like reports the earlier analysis (higher bad-effect ratings in women after allowing for dose per kilogram); in the editors' reading the difference may come from the outcome measure (area under the effect curve here, peak ratings there) and from the correction for multiple testing applied here, and it is listed for the senior author.

lines.q: Do some people feel MDMA more strongly than others?
lines.short: Yes. The biggest link was the amount per kilo of body weight. Given the same amount, lighter people got more per kilo, which went with stronger effects.
lines.but: That's one lab, with healthy young volunteers in a hospital. Most were trying MDMA for the first time.
how: 194 healthy young adults took MDMA in hospital, one set amount each time. On another day they took a dummy pill.
The amount per kilo of body weight went most with how strong it felt. Women and men didn't clearly differ once weight was counted, though an earlier report suggested women may feel more bad effects.
People who tend to worry, or who felt anxious and low just before, said they felt more anxious than calm people did. Open people felt closer to others.
Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do some people feel MDMA more strongly than others?

lines.statement: In emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre series and in case reports, seen only through two reviews (figures second-hand; the primary studies have not been read), acute methamphetamine toxicity presents with sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose reported frequency varies several-fold between studies and settings. A narrative review describes the common features, from case reports, as agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure, with coma and seizures less frequent, and deaths in case reports are attributed most often to pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia. For non-fatal presentations it gives agitation in about 20%, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4%, from a few series, some of them of amphetamine, without denominators. A systematic review of 23 studies (searches 1990–2017; 17 from the USA, 7 of them from one centre) could not pool any clinical feature, because the studies measured them inconsistently; study by study it lists tachycardia in 42% and 85% and hypertension in 6.4% and 69% of presentations (two studies), acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain (the review's table gives this study 171 patients), psychosis in 12% (two studies) to 80% (60 people at a psychiatric emergency service), agitation in 13% to 48%, aggression in 18% to 50% and suicidal thoughts or behaviour in 6% to 50%, mostly without stated denominators. Neither review gives a case fatality among presentations or compares fatal with non-fatal cases, so whether higher body temperature predicts death among people who present is not established; the narrative review cites forensic studies suggesting that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide. One series of amphetamine-related presentations (Perth, 2005) is a source for both reviews, so they are not independent.
lines.population: people presenting to emergency departments, psychiatric emergency services or trauma centres with acute methamphetamine toxicity (in some series, amphetamine)
lines.exposure: acute methamphetamine exposure (in some series, amphetamine or other stimulants)
lines.magnitude: Second-hand, mostly without denominators. Narrative review, non-fatal presentations: agitation about 20%, suicidal ideation 6–12%, acute psychosis 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis up to 14%, seizures 3–4%. Systematic review, study-level and not pooled: tachycardia 42% and 85%, hypertension 6.4% and 69% (two studies); acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain (171 patients in the review's table); psychosis 12% to 80%; agitation 13% to 48%; aggression 18% to 50%; suicidal thoughts or behaviour 6% to 50%. Not given by either review: case fatality among presentations, the proportion of deaths with other drugs detected, or any comparison of fatal with non-fatal cases.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive features from case reports and emergency chart reviews start low (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1). The claim now rests on two reviews: a narrative review (Cruickshank & Dyer, 2009), used as a pointer, and a systematic review (Sibanda et al., 2019) that searched four databases but pooled no clinical feature and reports no deaths (AMSTAR 2 critically low on its study card). Risk of bias, one level: the primary studies cannot be appraised through either review. Inconsistency, one level: study-level frequencies differ several-fold without explanation. Indirectness, one level: second-hand, and partly about amphetamine or other stimulants. Certainty very low (the floor). The two reviews share at least one primary series (Gray et al., 2007, amphetamine-related presentations in Perth), so they are not independent. Status replicated: independent series in different countries report the same features (tachycardia and hypertension in Perth and Taipei; psychosis or paranoia in Perth, Oregon, Seattle and Honolulu), and none reports their absence; the several-fold variation in how often they occur is part of the claim and is rated under inconsistency, not in the status label. The series shared by the two reviews (Gray et al., 2007) and the linked Perth and Oregon sets are counted once. Any statement about how often a feature occurs, about case fatality or about what predicts death needs the primary series read and, for prognosis, studies that compare fatal with non-fatal cases.

lines.q: What does a meth overdose look like?
lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies. How often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.
lines.q_on_site_now: What does meth poisoning look like?

lines.statement: In an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca (2017 to 2019; 6,877 self-selected respondents who had drunk with no more than two groups; Perkins et al., 2021), the setting of their last ceremony, as they described and rated it looking back, was associated with how much extreme fear they recalled and with difficulties afterwards, by small amounts. Of the 6,817 with a known setting, 52.1% had last drunk in an ayahuasca church (87% of them living in Brazil, and more than half having drunk over 200 times), 19.6% with traditional shamans and 28.3% in other settings; in these last two groups about two in three had drunk five times or fewer. Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of mental-health diagnoses, times drunk, years since the last drink, the three motivation scores and the other ceremony and support variables, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety (averages 3.4 to 3.9) went with less extreme fear or panic (−0.29 on a 0-to-10 scale, SE 0.07) and fewer difficulties in the weeks after (−0.13, SE 0.05); each point higher on a rating of the preparation offered (a chance to discuss one's history and concerns, and guidance on difficulties, before drinking) went with fewer later difficulties (−0.14, SE 0.03) but showed no detectable association with fear (−0.01, SE 0.04, p = 0.82). More fear went with more traditional practices (0.18 per practice, of up to 6), with drinking mostly in Amazonian countries other than Brazil (0.7), with therapeutic reasons for drinking (0.21 per reason) and with mental-health diagnoses (0.21 per diagnosis); less fear went with church features such as hymns or sermons (−0.38) and with each decade of age (−0.22). Fasting, offered at 35% of traditional settings, 26% of other settings and 2% of churches, showed no detectable difference in fear (−0.07 points on the 0-to-10 scale, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.15), later difficulties (−0.05, −0.21 to 0.11) or current distress (Kessler-10 −0.28, −0.69 to 0.13; editors' intervals): no difference was detected, which is not the same as showing there is none, since the fear interval runs from 0.29 points lower to 0.15 points higher. Fasting went with slightly higher ratings of mystical experience (1.7 points on a 9-to-90 scale) and of growth in well-being. Across the whole range of either rating, current distress differed by under 2 points on the 40-point Kessler scale (editors' arithmetic). Ratings and outcomes were reported by the same people at one sitting, on average 1.2 to 1.6 years after their last drink; the fear question did not say which session it meant, while the ceremony ratings concerned the last one; nothing was measured before ayahuasca, the amount and content of the brew were not recorded, no average or spread is given for the fear and difficulty measures, and the authors note that the sample may lean towards people with good experiences. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who have drunk ayahuasca, self-selected through ayahuasca organizations, retreat centres, churches and online groups (half of them church members, mostly in Brazil)
lines.exposure: Features of the last ceremony as the respondents described and rated them: church, traditional-shaman or other setting; support and safety; preparation offered; traditional or religious practices; fasting; country where they mostly drank
lines.comparator: Respondents who rated or described their last ceremony differently, adjusted for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink
lines.outcome: Extreme fear or panic during a session (0 to 10), difficulties in the weeks or months after, mystical-experience and growth ratings, and current distress (Kessler-10)
lines.magnitude: Adjusted B (SE): support and safety (per point, 1 to 4) extreme fear −0.29 (0.07), later difficulties −0.13 (0.05), Kessler-10 −0.62 (0.12); preparation offered (per point) later difficulties −0.14 (0.03), fear −0.01 (0.04, p = 0.82), Kessler-10 −0.25 (0.07); extreme fear: traditional practices 0.18 per practice, traditional country 0.7, therapeutic motivation 0.21, mental-health diagnoses 0.21, church features −0.38, age −0.22 per decade; fasting: fear −0.07 (0.11; 95% CI −0.29 to 0.15), later difficulties −0.05 (0.08; −0.21 to 0.11), Kessler-10 −0.28 (0.21; −0.69 to 0.13) (editors' intervals), mystical orientation 1.69 (0.64), growth 0.97 (0.37). Across a whole rating, under 2 Kessler-10 points (editors' arithmetic). The paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal; the fear coefficients are read as points on the 0-to-10 item, which assumes a linear model, and no mean or SD is given for the fear item or the difficulty count.
lines.reasoning: Cross-sectional survey, starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: companion and later papers from overlapping authors appear to draw on the same survey and would not count as independent replication. The authors' path model, selected on the same data, is not used.

lines.q: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?
lines.short: A little. Those who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled a bit less fear. They also reported fewer problems later.
lines.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear. Church hymns or sermons went with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?

lines.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the only prospective study among these sources found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults who planned an experience on their own initiative), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and with slightly higher well-being two weeks later (1.2 points on the well-being scale per standard deviation of the rating, p = 0.037, one of many coefficients in a model without correction for multiple tests; not significant at four weeks, p = 0.077); a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards in two yes-or-no questions that the authors combined into one variable, showed no statistically significant association with any acute measure (0.02), and the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink and for the motivation, ceremony and other support variables; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and no detectable difference in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with no statistically significant difference in either (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051, lower if anything) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). An opinion piece by the same group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same survey (266 people who completed four surveys), in which a 'therapeutic setting' (how it was recorded is not given) went with more peak or mystical-type experiences and trust in the people who would be present, rated beforehand, with less challenging ones; in the prospective study above, which appears to be the fuller report, a similar rating of the people and the place showed only a non-significant trend and a retreat or therapeutic setting no statistically significant association, so the preview is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. No study read here put people in different places or company on purpose to compare them. The same opinion piece states that, by 2018 and apart from a dose study, retrospective analyses and one 1969 study, controlled studies isolating contextual factors had not been done, and a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023, found no trial that compared settings (Estric et al., 2025; the trials were not appraised); in those trials, 12 kept two staff in the room throughout the session and five, published in 2023, one per participant, and rooms ranged from a hospital room left unchanged (4 trials) to one disguised as a living room or decorated; the review's authors judged that the decision to disguise the room, rather than only make it more pleasant, appeared to have been taken arbitrarily, without evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
lines.population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults who planned an experience on their own initiative (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
lines.exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
lines.comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
lines.outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
lines.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); setting component and well-being at two weeks 1.2 points per standard deviation (p = 0.037; at four weeks p = 0.077); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating); the paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal, so reading −0.29 as points on the fear item assumes a linear model. Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience, adjusted only for the other attributions: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2), and the associations it showed for trust and a therapeutic setting were not significant in the fuller report; a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) found no trial comparing settings up to December 2023. A trial analysis in which the quality of the therapeutic alliance correlated with emotional breakthrough and mystical-type experience (Murphy et al., 2022), cited by that review, has not been read.

lines.q: Do the place and the people around me affect a psychedelic trip?
lines.short: Maybe a little. In surveys, people who felt safe and supported reported slightly fewer hard moments.
lines.but: People rated this looking back. The one study that asked beforehand found only a weak link.
how: In a study that asked the day before, feeling good about the place and people went with slightly easier trips. But the link was weak and could be chance.
Almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca answered a survey. Those who felt safer and better supported at the ceremony reported a little less fear.
In a US survey, people who blamed a lack of support for their hardest trip said it was harder than people who did not.

No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, to compare them. A review of 25 trials found none either; some used plain hospital rooms, others disguised them as living rooms.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do the place and the people around me affect a psychedelic trip?

lines.statement: In 18 adult volunteers in Baltimore, USA (9 women and 9 men, mean age 28), who had used cannabis at some time but not in the previous 6 months by their own account and whose urine was negative before exposure, one hour seated in alternate seats beside six people smoking cannabis cigarettes as they wished, compared with each volunteer's own urine before exposure (there was no unexposed group), was followed by THCCOOH, a breakdown product the body makes from THC, in every volunteer's urine, but only rarely by a positive test at the US federal workplace cut-offs (Cone et al., 2015). Study conditions: a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling; in Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC and no ventilation (10.3 g smoked in the hour by the six people smoking); in Session 2, 11.3% THC and no ventilation (14.4 g); in Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, which the authors liken to home air-conditioning (16.5 g); a different six volunteers in each session, run in that fixed order at weekly or longer intervals; smoke was heavy in Sessions 1 and 2 and visible but greatly reduced in Session 3, and in Session 1 some of the people smoking stopped early after eye irritation, by their own account. Urine was collected from about 1 hour before to 34 hours after (250 specimens, including the 18 taken before exposure, of 252 scheduled) and tested with screening immunoassays at 20 and 50 ng/mL in five laboratories (one assay, CEDIA, also at 75 and 100 ng/mL) and by GC-MS, the confirmation cut-off being the 15 ng/mL of the SAMHSA Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs, whose screening cut-off is 50 ng/mL. THCCOOH became measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in all 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours. No specimen screened positive on the CEDIA assay at 100 or 75 ng/mL. At 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 specimens screened positive, on one of the five laboratories' assays only (the other four reported it negative): one woman's specimen 4 hours after Session 2, which held 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so that under the federal two-step rule (screen at 50, confirm at 15) 1 of the 18 volunteers would have had a positive with that assay and none with the others (editors' count). At the 20 ng/mL screening cut-off, which the authors say some private non-regulated programmes use, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3 numbered 12, 22 and 0 on DRI, 6, 8 and 0 on KIMS, 12, 22 and 1 on EMIT II Plus and 6, 12 and 0 on CEDIA; 12 of the 18 volunteers screened positive at least once on at least one assay (5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session), and 3 (with KIMS), 6 (with DRI or CEDIA) or 7 (with EMIT II Plus) of the 18 would have had a screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more by GC-MS, all of them in the unventilated sessions except one volunteer with EMIT II Plus (editors' counts from Table I). In all, 27 specimens from 7 volunteers reached 15 ng/mL (3, 22 and 2 by session; the paper's 10.8% of 250 counts the 18 specimens taken before exposure, so they are 27 of the 232 taken after it, 11.6%, editors' arithmetic), and peak values per volunteer ranged from 1.3 to 57.5 ng/mL. Screening positives at 20 ng/mL first appeared 1 to 4 hours after exposure and continued for 2 to 22 hours; the latest was in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL, positive on one assay); in the last pool, 30 to 34 hours after, no specimen screened positive on the four assays tabulated at 20 ng/mL or reached 15 ng/mL, although THCCOOH was still measurable in 12 of the 18. The authors' summary that positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure and confined to circumstances where exposure is obvious fits the 50 ng/mL screen, not a 20 ng/mL screen; 'immediately' understates positives that lasted up to 22 hours and one at 26 to 30 hours; and only obvious exposure was studied. A positive here is a urine result, a breakdown product of THC at or above a set level, not a measure of intoxication; this paper reports no measure of effects (blood, oral fluid, hair and effect measures were reserved for other reports). Differences between sessions cannot be put down to potency or ventilation alone, because the sessions ran in a fixed order with different people and Session 1 burned less cannabis. Funding: SAMHSA, which issues the federal guidelines whose cut-offs were tested; NIDA supplied the cannabis and funded one author; two authors are SAMHSA employees in its Division of Workplace Programs and the first author consults for that division. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 18 adult volunteers in Baltimore, USA (9 women, 9 men; mean age 28, range 20 to 45), recruited through advertisements, flyers and word of mouth and paid, who had used cannabis at some time but not in the previous 6 months by their own account, with urine negative for cannabis and other drugs at screening and admission and no or minimal tobacco use; six per session, each in one session only
lines.exposure: One hour seated in alternate seats beside six people smoking cannabis cigarettes as they wished, in a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling (study conditions): Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC, no ventilation, 10.3 g smoked in all; Session 2, 11.3% THC, no ventilation, 14.4 g; Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, 16.5 g
lines.comparator: Each volunteer's own urine about 1 hour before exposure (all negative by GC-MS and immunoassay); no unexposed group and no placebo condition; the three sessions differ in potency, ventilation, amount smoked, people and week, in a fixed order
lines.outcome: Urinary THCCOOH by GC-MS (confirmation cut-off 15 ng/mL) and screening immunoassay results at 20, 50, 75 and 100 ng/mL in specimens collected for 34 hours after exposure: specimens and volunteers screening positive at each cut-off, and those whose screening positive would be confirmed at 15 ng/mL
lines.magnitude: Cone et al. (2015), 18 volunteers, 250 specimens (18 before exposure, 232 after): screening positives at 100 and 75 ng/mL (CEDIA only), 0 of 250; at 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 (printed 0.4%; one of five laboratories' assays), 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so 1 of 18 volunteers positive under the federal 50 and 15 ng/mL cut-offs with that assay (Wilson 95% interval 1.0% to 25.8%, editors' calculation) and 0 of 18 with the other assays; at 20 ng/mL, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3: DRI 12, 22, 0; KIMS 6, 8, 0; EMIT II Plus 12, 22, 1; CEDIA 6, 12, 0 (34, 14, 35 and 18 of 250 in all, editors' sums); volunteers with at least one 20 ng/mL screening positive on any of the four assays, 12 of 18 (66.7%; 43.7% to 83.7%; 5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session; editors' count); volunteers with a 20 ng/mL screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more: KIMS 3, DRI 6, CEDIA 6, EMIT II Plus 7 of 18 (editors' count); specimens at 15 ng/mL or more, 27 (3, 22 and 2 by session) from 7 of 18 volunteers (38.9%; 20.3% to 61.4%), that is 27 of 232 specimens taken after exposure (11.6%; 8.1% to 16.4%) against the printed 10.8% of 250; peak THCCOOH per volunteer by session, mean (range) 11.2 (1.9 to 20.1), 28.3 (5.5 to 57.5) and 7.5 (1.3 to 15.5) ng/mL; THCCOOH measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in 18 of 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours and in 12 of 18 in the 30-to-34-hour pool; latest screening positive in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL), none in the 30-to-34-hour pools (editors' count). No unexposed group, so no difference from unexposed people can be given.
lines.reasoning: A controlled exposure in volunteers without a placebo or unexposed condition, its three conditions run in a fixed order with different people, does not meet the rule under which within-person laboratory studies start high (placebo-controlled, with randomized or counterbalanced order); what happened to the volunteers' urine is rated as a description of these conditions (METHODS §6.3), starting low. Indirectness −1 (an extreme, obvious exposure in a small sealed room, while the question is about other people's smoke in general) and imprecision −1 (18 volunteers, 6 per condition) bring it to very low, the floor. Not rated down for risk of bias: the urine results are objective, complete and fully tabulated, and the editors' recount from Table I reproduces every printed count; the serious risk of bias of the comparisons between sessions (ROBINS-I; fixed order, different volunteers) is not used, because the claim does not attribute differences to potency or ventilation. Worded as 'describes': the exposure plainly put THCCOOH into urine (every pre-exposure specimen negative, every volunteer measurable within 3 hours), but the claim's point is how many tests would read positive at each cut-off, a count under these conditions. The authors' 'rare' is adopted only for the 50 ng/mL screen, with the counts at 20 ng/mL beside it; 'only where exposure is obvious' is not adopted, because only obvious exposure was studied. The counts of volunteers and of confirmed positives are editors' counts from Table I (minus signs read from the rendered pages and from the PDF's symbol font), to be recomputed by the second reader. Status single study: the authors say earlier passive-exposure studies, mostly with weaker cannabis, also found THC metabolites in non-smokers' urine, but those were not read here. Funding by SAMHSA, which issues the guidelines tested, and the authors' ties to it are given in the statement. Amounts appear only as study conditions, and nothing is phrased as advice about tests.

lines.q: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?
lines.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
lines.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once, and for 3 to 7, a lab check would have confirmed it.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.

lines.statement: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read at the sites, after infrared spectroscopy of the same sample and with one combined result recorded, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples from five of the sites, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 times or more the concentrations at which it detected the others (editors' calculation) (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). A report relayed second-hand by Laing et al. concluded that newer benzodiazepines appear to be detected by similar strips, etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than other NPS benzodiazepines, still within the range useful for drug checking (Shapiro et al., 2020), so the sources disagree on whether these strips react to etizolam at all; differences in lots or test conditions may explain it, but this was not shown. Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey, Canada (2018 to 2020), of which 153 had confirmatory laboratory results; benzodiazepines in water in a second laboratory
lines.exposure: BTNX benzodiazepine urine test strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL) used on dissolved drug at the sites after FTIR of the same sample, with one combined result recorded; the same maker's strip in pure solutions
lines.comparator: Confirmatory laboratory testing (GC–MS, LC-MS or qNMR) for NPS benzodiazepines; known content of prepared solutions
lines.outcome: Detection of NPS benzodiazepines (sensitivity), false positives, and detection of individual benzodiazepines in water
lines.magnitude: Laing et al. (153 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results; 6 with only typical benzodiazepines removed): strips 15/24 NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%; Wilson 42.7–78.8%, editors' calculation), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20/129 negatives positive (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); 87.5% (n = 8) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam; 50.0% (n = 16; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone; FTIR 2/24 (false-negative rate 91.7%), false-positive rate 3.9%; either method 17/24 detected, 23 false positives. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024): limits 0.1 µg/mL (diazepam, alprazolam) and 0.25 µg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); etizolam negative from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 to 100 times or more those limits (editors' calculation). Second-hand (Shapiro et al., 2020, via Laing et al.): similar strips appear to detect etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than flualprazolam and flubromazolam.
lines.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; Laing et al.'s agreement figures are accuracy evidence with high risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), so two levels for risk of bias and one each for indirectness and imprecision take it to the floor of very low. Rated as worded. Status replicated: independent teams (British Columbia; NIST) both found etizolam poorly detected; Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round; the Shapiro et al. report is second-hand and not counted.

lines.q: Do benzo test strips catch etizolam and other newer benzos?
lines.short: Not reliably. At one drug-checking service, strips caught newer benzos in 15 of 24 samples that had them, and just 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.
lines.but: A lab checked only some samples, not picked at random. Some were chosen because of a suspected benzo overdose.
how: At eight health sites, samples were tested with strips, and a lab checked some of them.
Strips caught 7 of 8 samples with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam. With etizolam alone, they caught only 8 of 16.
They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which the lab found none; what set those off wasn't reported.
The same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam, even at 40 or more times the level at which it caught other benzos. An earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up.
