lines.statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, read positive in nearly all residue samples with at least the strip's listed amount of xylazine, read positive on every strip in pure solutions only from 2.5 times that amount, and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%; the one miss had 2 µg/mL) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not at that concentration, the only one tested, so at that level these strips would not show them; higher concentrations, as from dissolved powders, were not tested (Sisco, Nestadt, et al., 2024). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
lines.population: 100 drug residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment in two US states, and pure xylazine and 76 other compounds in water
lines.exposure: One production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips, two strips per sample, read in a laboratory; a later version with a different antibody in a second study
lines.comparator: GC-MS/MS quantitation of xylazine in each residue sample; known content of prepared solutions
lines.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity on residue samples, the lowest concentration giving consistent positives, and reactions to other compounds
lines.magnitude: Sisco, Nestadt, et al. (2024), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%; the one miss at 2 µg/mL); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). Pure xylazine: 15/15 positive at 2.5 µg/mL and above; 3/15 at 1 µg/mL (12 faint); 7/15 at 0.5 µg/mL (8 faint); 0/15 at 0.1 µg/mL. Cross-reactivity at 100 µg/mL only: lidocaine alone of 76 other compounds. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.
lines.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence on real residues against quantitative GC-MS/MS starts high; one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded. The two studies share their first author and laboratory and test different versions of the strip, so the status is replicated by the same team; the newer version rests on one laboratory study in pure solutions (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024, re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round).

lines.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
lines.but: One batch of strips was read in a lab. The samples were residues from used equipment, not powders.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.

lines.statement: In adults with moderate or severe PTSD who had stopped their psychiatric medicines (two phase 3 trials from one sponsor: 90 adults with severe PTSD in MAPP1, 104 with moderate to severe PTSD in MAPP2), MDMA given in three sessions within an intensive manualized therapy, compared with an inactive placebo given with the same therapy, lowered clinician-rated PTSD symptom scores (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80, baseline means about 44 and 39) at 18 weeks by 11.9 points more in MAPP1 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 points more in MAPP2 (4.1 to 13.7); both arms improved substantially (in MAPP2, by 23.7 and 14.8 points). Analyses that kept scores recorded after people stopped treatment, a worst-case imputation of MAPP1's missing scores and a tipping-point analysis in MAPP2 still showed a significant difference (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2's supplement). Among completers (MAPP1) and those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2), 67% vs 32% and 71% vs 48% no longer met PTSD criteria; counting everyone randomized (for MAPP1, everyone dosed), 61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% (editors' calculation). Functional impairment improved slightly more with MDMA (SDS difference 1.2 points on a 0 to 10 scale in MAPP2, and 1.4 in MAPP1 by the amended study report as the sponsor's briefing document gives it). The two trials share their sponsor, design and therapy manual, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors; in MAPP2, the only trial that asked, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group at the end of the study, MAPP1 did not assess blinding, and neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, so how much of the difference is due to MDMA itself is uncertain; the trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the only later data, a single observational follow-up visit analysed in the FDA's briefing document, were judged by the FDA not designed to evaluate durability; no trial in the sources read compares MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused psychotherapy. The FDA's reviewers, re-tabulating the sponsor's study reports, give the same estimates and call the changes clinically meaningful (their threshold is 10 points), while judging that functional unblinding and expectation bias, which they cannot quantify, probably affected them, the in-session monitors probably knowing allocation too; the FDA's advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
lines.population: Adults with DSM-5 PTSD of at least 6 months, CAPS-5 of 35 or more (MAPP1) or 28 or more (MAPP2), after washout of psychiatric medicines; people with current substance use disorders (MAPP1) or most substance use disorders (MAPP2), personality disorders or cardiovascular disease excluded, and in MAPP2 also people at high suicide risk
lines.exposure: MDMA in three 8-hour sessions about a month apart, within a manualized therapy of three preparatory and nine integration sessions with a two-person team
lines.comparator: Inactive placebo with the identical therapy
lines.outcome: Change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (primary); loss of PTSD diagnosis; SDS functional impairment
lines.magnitude: MAPP1 (de jure MMRM, n = 89): difference 11.9 CAPS-5 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), d 0.91 (0.44 to 1.37) as printed (it equals the completers' raw difference of 10.5 points over their pooled SD; the model difference over the same SD gives about 1.03, editors' calculation); registry least-squares means −24.5 vs −12.64. MAPP2 (n = 103): −23.7 (−26.94 to −20.44) vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28); difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), d 0.7. Loss of diagnosis among completers (MAPP1) and those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2): 28/42 (67%) vs 12/37 (32%) and 37/52 (71.2%) vs 20/42 (47.6%); with everyone randomized as denominator (for MAPP1, the 46 and 44 dosed; editors' calculation): 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 points, 14.3 to 52.9) and 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8). Remission 14/42 vs 2/37 and 24/52 vs 9/42. SDS: MAPP2 difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14); MAPP1 P = 0.0116, d 0.43 (−0.01 to 0.88) in the publication, but −1.36 (−2.46 to −0.25), P = 0.0167, in the FDA's table from the clinical study report. The FDA's tables give the same CAPS-5 estimates (MAPP2 P = 0.0004) and count 91 randomized in MAPP1 (46 and 45), of whom 90 were dosed; the sponsor's briefing document gives the same SDS difference. Sensitivity analyses (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2 supplement): MAPP1 de facto difference −12.04 (−17.46 to −6.62), worst-case imputation P = 0.0293; MAPP2 de facto −8.93 (−13.69 to −4.17); MAPP2 result significant until the missing placebo values are shifted 28 points toward improvement. Responder P values are nominal (MAPP2 response P = 0.0708).
lines.reasoning: Two randomized, prospectively registered phase 3 trials (193 in the modified intention-to-treat sets, 90 and 103), starting high. Risk of bias, two levels (very serious): in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants very probably knew their group (in MAPP2's end-of-study survey 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it, mostly from effects felt or not felt; MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only anecdotes); neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, and the assessors' guesses were not recorded. This bias runs toward a larger difference (expectation on MDMA, disappointment on placebo, which the MAPP2 authors themselves name as a possible reason for the 8 vs 1 placebo dropouts, 5 of them after the first session); it is shared by both trials, so their agreement does not reduce it; and its size cannot be estimated from these papers, while the differences it would have to explain are of a comparable order (8.9 and 11.9 points, lower limits 4.1 and 6.3). METHODS §6.3 rates down when the biases that remain could plausibly change the estimate materially, as here (the FDA's reviewers reach the same view, add that the in-session monitors probably knew allocation too and say the bias cannot be quantified, and 9 of the 11 voting members of its advisory committee judged the data unable to show effectiveness); that the bias is unlikely to explain all of the difference argues against very low, not for moderate (the first reader's strict reading; both second readers). The sponsor's oversight of data collection, analysis and interpretation is carried by the status (replicated by the same team), not by a further level. Missing outcome data are not a further reason to rate down: analyses keeping scores recorded after people stopped treatment, MAPP1's worst-case imputation and MAPP2's tipping-point analysis all kept a significant difference (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2 supplement); they do not address unblinding. Inconsistency not rated down: both trials found differences in the same direction with overlapping intervals (d 0.91 and 0.7). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial populations, to the comparison with placebo plus the same therapy and to 18 weeks. Imprecision not rated down: both intervals exclude no difference, though their lower ends (4.1 and 6.3 points) are small relative to the 10-point change agreed with the FDA as clinically meaningful for an individual. Publication bias not rated down: both registered phase 3 trials are published. The relation stays 'reduces': randomization supports causal language about the package that was assigned (MDMA against placebo within the same therapy), which the site uses for randomized evidence at low certainty; how much of the difference is due to MDMA's pharmacology is the question of the contested claim in section 14.

lines.q: Does MDMA-assisted therapy help PTSD more than therapy with a dummy pill?
lines.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA with standard talking therapy.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does MDMA-assisted therapy help PTSD more than therapy with a dummy pill?

lines.statement: In US youths aged 12.5 to 18 in a national household panel (the National Survey of Parents and Youth: three cohorts aged 9 to 18 from a probability sample of US households, interviewed at home four times between November 1999 and June 2004; 8,117 youths in the first round, with a 65% response rate, and 5,126 in the fourth), more recalled exposure to the US National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign compared with less recalled exposure did not detectably reduce marijuana (cannabis) use or first use, or strengthen antidrug intentions, beliefs, norms or confidence in refusing marijuana (Hornik et al., 2008). Congress appropriated nearly $1 billion for the campaign for 1998–2004; it bought advertising from September 1999 to June 2004, 64% of its rating points on TV and radio. The evaluation was mandated by Congress and paid from the campaign's appropriation, supervised by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, which also funded the authors. There was no unexposed group: 94% of youths recalled at least one antidrug ad a month, so the evaluation compared youths who recalled more with youths who recalled less, after propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders. Self-reported marijuana use among youths aged 12.5 to 18 did not change from 2000 to 2004: lifetime use 23.6% and 23.5% (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8) and past-30-day use 7.8% and 8.2% (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2), weighted percentages whose yearly numbers of youths are not printed; of four antidrug views among youths who had not used marijuana, only an index of beliefs and attitudes rose (6.3 points, 0.4 to 12.2). At the same interview, youths who recalled more exposure held no more antidrug views (gammas −0.02 to 0.03, every interval including no association). Among youths who had not used marijuana, more exposure went, at the next round 12 to 18 months later, with fewer saying they definitely would not use it (82.3%, 78.2% and 78.4% across rising general exposure; gamma −0.07, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.01) and with weaker antidrug norms (gamma −0.05, −0.08 to −0.02, for recall of specific ads). First use by the next round was 10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across rising general exposure (gamma 0.07, −0.01 to 0.15, not significant when pooled), and more first use with more exposure was significant only from the third round (July 2002 to June 2003) to the fourth (gamma 0.11, 0.00 to 0.22), which the authors call barely significant. Of 80 subgroup analyses of later outcomes, 20 were significant, 19 of them unfavourable; none of the tests is reported as corrected for multiple comparisons. The authors conclude that the campaign is unlikely to have had favourable effects, and judge the support for unfavourable effects tentative, not definitive. Exposure and use were self-reported, and with no group that missed the campaign the design cannot show what would have happened without it: effects shared by everyone, spread through friends, or occurring before the first round, which began with the full launch, would be missed. As the authors describe two school surveys, these showed some fall in youth marijuana use over these years, which this survey did not, and larger falls in tobacco and alcohol use. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: US youths aged 12.5 to 18 at outcome measurement in the National Survey of Parents and Youth, a household panel from a stratified four-stage national probability sample (90 primary sampling units): three cohorts aged 9 to 18 interviewed at home four times, November 1999 to June 2004 (8,117, 6,516, 5,854 and 5,126 youths in rounds 1 to 4; 65% first-round response; 86% to 93% of still-eligible youths reinterviewed); association analyses restricted to youths who had not used marijuana
lines.exposure: Recalled exposure to the National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign's advertising: general (how often antidrug ads were seen or heard in recent months, by medium) and specific (prompted recall of up to 4 TV and 2 radio campaign ads aired in the 2 months before the interview)
lines.comparator: Youths recalling less exposure (general: under 4, 4 to 11, 12 or more a month; specific: under 1, 1 to 3, 4 to 11, 12 or more a month); no unexposed group; for trends, the same population in 2000
lines.outcome: Self-reported lifetime, past-year and past-30-day marijuana use; first use of marijuana by the next round; intention not to use marijuana, and indices of antimarijuana beliefs and attitudes, social norms and self-efficacy
lines.magnitude: Hornik et al. (2008). Trends among youths aged 12.5–18, 2000 to 2004 (weighted percentages; yearly numbers not printed): lifetime marijuana use 23.6 to 23.5 (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8); past year 17.1 to 16.7 (−0.4, −2.6 to 1.9); past 30 days 7.8 to 8.2 (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2); among youths who had not used marijuana, definitely not intending to use 86.7 to 87.5 (0.8, −1.0 to 2.6); index changes: beliefs and attitudes 6.3 (0.4 to 12.2), self-efficacy 2.4 (−3.3 to 8.2), social norms 1.2 (−5.1 to 7.3). Cross-sectional gammas −0.02 to 0.03, all intervals including 0. Lagged gammas pooled across round pairs: intention with general exposure −0.07 (−0.13 to −0.01); social norms with specific exposure −0.05 (−0.08 to −0.02); first use with general exposure 0.07 (−0.01 to 0.15) (10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across under 4, 4–11 and 12 or more exposures a month); first use with specific exposure printed as −0.02 (−0.13 to 0.08), although its percentages rise from 10.8% to 13.2%. First use with general exposure by round pair: 0.08 (−0.05 to 0.20), 0.01 (−0.11 to 0.13) and 0.11 (0.00 to 0.22) for rounds 1–2, 2–3 and 3–4. Subgroups: 3 of 80 cross-sectional and 20 of 80 lagged gammas significant (19 of the 20 unfavourable). No comparison with an unexposed group, so no effect of the campaign against no campaign can be given.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence (naturally occurring differences in recalled exposure within one national panel, with no unexposed group) starts low and is not rated down further, giving low. Rated as worded: no detectable favourable change with more recalled exposure, and no fall in use over the campaign years. Whether the campaign changed anything compared with no campaign is not rated, because almost every youth was exposed, which the statement says. The unfavourable associations at the next round are reported, not rated as a separate claim: they come from many tests not reported as corrected, appear only for some outcomes and periods (more first use only from round 3 to round 4), and the authors themselves judge their support tentative; the printed gamma for specific exposure and first use (−0.02) does not fit its rising percentages and is not used. Status single study: one national panel; the authors mention a smaller study of the campaign in two cities over 6 months that reported favourable effects, not read here.

lines.q: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?
lines.short: No sign they did. Congress put nearly $1 billion into the campaign, but teen cannabis use stayed flat, and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
lines.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens had ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.
lines.q_on_site_now: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?

lines.statement: Crack and powder are the same drug in two forms. A 1996 narrative review puts most differences between them down to the route each form allows and the speed and amount of cocaine it delivers, and to the amounts people use, rather than to the form itself; a 2017 systematic review names crack's own pharmacology and routes, and the marginalized circumstances of many people who use it, as possible explanations without testing them. No source read tests crack against powder with route, amount and circumstances accounted for. Powder cannot be smoked because it breaks down at the temperature needed to vaporize it, while the base form (crack) can, so to some extent the form sets the route: crack is smoked, powder is snorted or injected. Once in the blood, the 1996 review describes the two forms as eliminated and broken down alike, with peak levels in venous blood about 5 minutes after smoking or injecting against about 30 to 40 minutes after snorting (second-hand from studies not read here; Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). In US household surveys of 1995–1998, among 762 people who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months, each of seven dependence features was reported more often by the 190 who had started crack (some of whom had also just started powder) than by the 572 who had started powder and never used crack: weighted occurrence in the past year about 18% to 32% against about 5% to 12%, or about 2.5 to 4.4 times as often by the editors' reading of the figure. The summary odds ratio across features, adjusted for sex, age, race, daily drinking, daily tobacco smoking, injecting and the number of days cocaine was used, was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5), and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for a further 93 people who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; without the term for days of use the estimate was about 2.3 to 3.7, reported without intervals (Chen & Anthony, 2004). Those estimates come from one interview, with use, form and problems all self-reported and no measure of how people differed before they started; the authors say a greater susceptibility among people who start crack cannot be ruled out, and they fitted the model with and without days of use because dependence itself may raise use, so adjusting for it may remove part of a real difference. The 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles pooled only comparisons of crack use against people not using drugs or the general population, never against powder. In its narrative synthesis, comparisons of people using crack with people using other forms of cocaine were described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies), and as showing no difference for 10 other diagnoses (5 studies); single studies found more anorexia and insomnia and less suicidal thinking with crack, and more violence toward others than among people snorting cocaine but not more than among people injecting it; the review neither pooled nor tested these comparisons. Its authors judge crack not a plausible direct cause of the infections and violence linked with its use, reading crack use as a facilitator or marker of risk behaviours and risk environments, and call it unclear for mental health whether crack use is a cause, a consequence or comorbid (Butler et al., 2017). The 1996 review, whose evidence on patterns of use comes from uncontrolled surveys and treatment, street and jail samples, mostly of the mid-1980s to early 1990s, reports that people who smoke or inject cocaine typically use it more often and in larger amounts than people who snort it (one Miami sample found the largest amounts among people snorting), that people who smoke crack reach regular use sooner than people who snort or inject, and that smoking or injecting goes with a faster onset of problems and earlier treatment; its statement that differences disappear once the amount used is held constant rests partly on two sets of meeting proceedings published before crack appeared. No comparison of crack with powder in the sources read adjusts for the amount taken per occasion, for illegal drugs other than cocaine, or for income, housing or the policing people met; the household survey adjusts for daily drinking, daily smoking, injecting and days of use. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
lines.population: People in US households, 1995–1998 surveys: 762 who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months (572 powder only; 190 recent crack, some of whom had also just started powder) and 93 who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; the samples of a 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles on crack use, mostly marginalized high-risk groups in the USA, Brazil and Canada; the treatment, survey, laboratory and administrative sources of a 1996 narrative review
lines.exposure: Crack (smoked cocaine base), compared with cocaine hydrochloride powder (snorted or injected)
lines.comparator: People who had started powder cocaine and never used crack; in the 2017 review's pooled estimates, people not using drugs or the general population (crack against other forms of cocaine only in its narrative synthesis)
lines.outcome: Dependence features, mental-health and other health outcomes, and patterns of use
lines.magnitude: Chen & Anthony (2004), weighted past-year occurrence of seven dependence features: about 5% to 12% among 572 people who had started powder only; about 18% to 32% among 190 who had recently started crack and about 11% to 33% among 93 who had started crack after two or more years of powder use (the group ranges are the first reader's readings of a figure that prints no values). Unadjusted odds ratios, recent crack against powder only: reduced activities 5.6 (1.9 to 15.9), tolerance 4.8 (1.8 to 12.6), inability to cut down 4.0 (1.9 to 8.7), emotional problems 3.5 (1.6 to 7.7), salience 3.4 (1.5 to 7.7), using more than intended 3.1 (1.4 to 7.0), health problems 3.0 (0.9 to 9.7). Adjusted summary across the seven features: 1.9 (1.4 to 2.5) for recent crack and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for crack after two or more years of powder; about 2.3 to 3.7 without the days-of-use term (no intervals). These are odds ratios although the paper calls them relative risks; from the figure the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 2.5 to 4.4 for recent crack and about 1.5 to 3.3 for crack after powder (editors' calculation from the figure readings). Butler et al. (2017): no pooled crack-versus-powder estimate; 12 studies mixed and 5 showing no difference, none pooled or tested by the review; one study found more violence toward others with crack than with snorted cocaine, and no difference from injected cocaine. Hatsukami & Fischman (1996), second-hand: two thirds of people smoking crack used daily against 18% of people snorting powder, among people interviewed in treatment, street, jail or prison settings in New York City in 1988–1989; in the 1991 national survey, crack use was 52.5% among people who used cocaine frequently and 17.5% among those who used it infrequently (neither defined), injecting 24.3% against 9.3%.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and indirectness −1 take it below the floor: very low. The claim is worded as an association and is rated as one (METHODS §6.3). Status mixed: a population survey finds an excess of dependence features with crack that shrinks after adjustment, while the one systematic review covering the same question describes the comparisons as mixed and pools none, and the 1996 review attributes the differences to route, amount and context without testing them. The three sources are not independent: the 2017 review includes Chen & Anthony (2004) in its narrative synthesis and cites the 1996 review as background, so they are counted once. Not used, following the study cards: a causal effect of smoking crack, the 1996 review's figures as measurements, its gateway reading of sequence data, and any crack-versus-powder difference in physical harms, for which the sources read give only second-hand, unadjusted figures.

lines.q: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?
lines.short: Possibly, though it's the same drug. People new to crack reported each sign of dependence more often: about 18 to 32 in 100, against 5 to 12 for powder.
lines.but: Each person was asked once, so the surveys cannot show that crack itself is the reason.
how: Powder can't be smoked; crack is. A 1996 review links most differences to how each is taken, how fast and how much cocaine that delivers, and how much people use, not the form itself.
In US surveys from 1995 to 1998, about 18 to 32 in 100 people who had just started crack reported each sign of dependence. For people who had just started powder, it was 5 to 12 in 100.
After allowing for how many days people had used, and for age, drinking, smoking and injecting, the gap was smaller but did not go away.
A review of 302 studies found comparisons of crack with other cocaine mixed. Its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it.
lines.q_on_site_now: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?

lines.statement: The US National Comorbidity Survey (1990–1992; household sample aged 15–54; structured CIDI interview) reported, for each drug class separately, the proportion of people who had ever used it who had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for dependence, with non-medical use of stimulants other than cocaine counted as one class. Among people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (15.3% of the population; dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine are the examples given), 11.2% (SE 1.6; about 8.1% to 14.3%, editors' calculation) had ever met the criteria, against 31.9% for tobacco (no standard error; tobacco use came from a separate 1991 survey and dependence was assessed for daily smoking in a subsample), 15.4% for alcohol, 16.7% for cocaine, 23.1% for heroin and 9.1% for cannabis. Such proportions are taken at a single interview among everyone who had ever used, including once (the dependence questions were asked only of people reporting more than a few occasions of use), and do not account for people who started recently; the data are three decades old, grouped across stimulants and based on DSM-III-R criteria. The source calls the class psychostimulants other than cocaine; it includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants. A 2007 Australian national household survey (8,841 people aged 16–85; response 60%; WMH-CIDI 3.0 interview) measured something different. Its outcome was broader, DSM-IV stimulant abuse or dependence, in a stimulant class the paper does not define. Of 579 people who had used stimulants, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had met the criteria by the interview. A survival analysis, which uses the years since each person first used and so allows for people who had started recently, estimated a cumulative probability of 50.4% (no interval given) of developing the disorder within 14 years of first use, 12.2% within the first year. The criteria were asked only of people who had used at least five times, and the authors note that counting abuse as well as dependence gives higher estimates than studies of dependence alone. The two surveys therefore measure different quantities and cannot be compared directly, and neither gives a figure for methamphetamine alone.
lines.population: US household (noninstitutionalized) population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992 who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically; Australian household population aged 16–85 in 2007 who had ever used stimulants (class not defined)
lines.exposure: lifetime extramedical use of psychostimulants other than cocaine, including prescription stimulants used without or beyond a prescription (US); lifetime use of stimulants, class not defined (Australia)
lines.outcome: lifetime DSM-III-R dependence, as a proportion at interview (US); lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence, as a proportion at interview and as a cumulative probability by years since first use (Australia)
lines.magnitude: US NCS (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): proportion ever dependent (DSM-III-R) among people who had ever used extramedically: psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (SE 1.6; editors' 95% CI about 8.1% to 14.3%), from 15.3% lifetime use and 1.7% lifetime dependence in the population; tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6). Stimulants by age: 13.5% (15–24), 13.9% (25–34), 7.7% (35–44), 6.5% (45–54); by sex: men 9.7%, women 13.3% (Tables 4–5). Australia 2007 (NSMHWB; weighted; stimulant class not defined; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) of 579 people who had used stimulants had ever met the criteria at interview; cumulative probability by years since first use (discrete-time survival analysis, no interval) 12.2% within the first year and 50.4% within 14 years; among those who developed the disorder, half did so within about 3 years (IQR 1–5) of first use.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions and a cumulative probability in survey populations): starts low. Risk of bias, one level, for the Australian figures only (60% response, recalled timing, unclear denominator); the US figures are not downgraded (JBI low; the authors discuss frame, deaths and self-report, pp. 263–265). Indirectness, two levels: neither survey isolates methamphetamine, the US class includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants, and the Australian class is undefined and its outcome includes abuse; the criteria are DSM-III-R (1990–1992) and DSM-IV (2007). Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the two figures measure different things: a proportion ever dependent among everyone who had ever used, at one interview, against a projected cumulative probability of abuse or dependence by 14 years after first use. Certainty very low. The tobacco proportion is less comparable than the others: it combines tobacco use from a separate 1991 survey with dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample, and has no standard error. Status single study: the two surveys measure different quantities (see inconsistency), so they neither replicate nor contradict each other, and each figure rests on one survey; the four- to five-fold gap between them has candidate explanations (abuse counted, undefined class, a denominator that may exclude people with few uses, country and decade) that have not been tested. Imprecision not downgraded: the US proportion has a standard error and the Australian 45.7% an interval; the 50.4% has none, so its precision cannot be judged, which changes nothing at the floor. The US authors conclude from their figures that many, perhaps most, people who use a drug do not become dependent (p. 265); for stimulants, the Australian survival estimate (about half within 14 years, abuse included) shows that this conclusion depends on the measure and on how the outcome is defined.

lines.q: How many people who use stimulants like meth get hooked?
lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.
lines.q_on_site_now: How many people who use stimulants like meth become dependent?

lines.statement: In eight men given MDMA 75 mg and 125 mg on separate days in a randomized, double-blind crossover, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.81 times higher (236.4 against 130.9 ug/L) and a 24-hour exposure 1.97 times higher (2623.7 against 1331.5 ug x h/L), so blood levels rose more than the dose did (de la Torre et al., 2000; ratios from the printed means). Clearance outside the kidneys fell from 74.0 to 38.1 L/h while clearance by the kidneys did not change, and across the five dose levels from 50 to 150 mg, with different men at 50, 100 and 150 mg, the same eight men at 75 and 125 mg, and only two men at each of the lowest and highest, the 24-hour exposure ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug x h/L, so differences between men are mixed in with the dose. The authors give two explanations, saturation of MDMA's breakdown (which they say cannot be excluded) and MDMA's blocking of the enzyme CYP2D6 that breaks it down, and state that the observations were retrospective and the studies were not designed to detect this. The authors' abstract goes further, concluding that this holds for the whole population whatever the CYP2D6 genotype and that small increases in the amount taken give disproportionate rises in blood level, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity; the dose comparison was made in men with normal CYP2D6 only and no toxicity outcome was measured. In a later study of 15 men, one dose of MDMA switched CYP2D6 off, and the enzyme's activity had not fully recovered after 10 days (O'Mathúna et al., 2008); this fits the second explanation, as does the small difference between people with and without a working enzyme (Schmid et al., 2016). The authors of the 2008 study infer, without giving a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts the effect, bodies that differ) and some take more. None of these studies tested people who took more because they felt little: the amounts were fixed and given to healthy men in a laboratory, and what they show is that a larger single amount gave a larger rise in blood level than the amount itself. Second doses taken 2 or 24 hours after a first are covered in the library's separate claim on acute tolerance.
lines.population: Healthy adult men with earlier MDMA experience in laboratory studies: 14 men (8 in a randomized crossover at 75 and 125 mg; 6 in a pilot at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and, for the mechanism, 15 men in a probe-drug study
lines.exposure: A larger single dose of MDMA (study conditions: 75 mg and 125 mg, and 50, 100 and 150 mg in the pilot, by mouth)
lines.comparator: The same eight men at the smaller dose, with dose-normalized exposure as the yardstick
lines.outcome: Peak and 24-hour exposure of MDMA in plasma, dose-normalized exposure, kidney and non-kidney clearance, and recovery of urinary MDMA and HMMA
lines.magnitude: 75 mg against 125 mg, 8 men (de la Torre et al., 2000): peak 130.9 (SD 38.6) against 236.4 (58.0) ug/L; AUC(0-24 h) 1331.5 (646.0) against 2623.7 (572.9) ug x h/L; dose-normalized AUC 17.8 (8.6) against 21.0 (4.6), paired t test of AUC(0-infinity) P<0.03, 90% interval of the within-person ratio -0.3 to 89.3%; non-renal clearance 74.0 against 38.1 L/h (P<0.03); total clearance 86.9 (74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h as printed; unchanged MDMA in urine 71.2 (13.7) against 169.6 (69.5) micromol. Across 50 to 150 mg, 24-hour exposure 100.1 and 813.9 (two men at 50 mg) against 5132.8 and 5232.0 (two men at 150 mg); Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized exposure P<0.1. Editors' calculation from the printed means: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the exposure.
lines.reasoning: The 75 against 125 mg comparison is a randomized, double-blind, within-person crossover and starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -2 (eight men, an interval reaching zero, two men per dose in the wider range) give very low. Status single-study: one study shows the dose comparison; the probe-drug and genotype studies bear on the mechanism, not on dose proportionality. The claim describes the blood levels in fixed-dose laboratory conditions; it is not guidance on any amount.

lines.q: Does taking more MDMA raise blood levels more than you'd expect?
lines.short: Yes, it seems so: a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher, and about twice the total over the day.
lines.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
The kidneys cleared MDMA at the same pace at both doses; the rest of the body cleared it about half as fast at the larger one.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

People can feel little from an amount for several reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ. Some take more. These studies didn't test that.
lines.q_on_site_now: Why does taking more raise blood levels more than expected?
